title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
tagline: Greedy shortest paths from a source on non-negative weighted graphs, via a priority queue.

intuition.analogy: Water flowing from a spring through pipes of different lengths reaches the nearest junctions first. At any moment, the closest not-yet-reached junction's distance is final — nothing can offer it a shorter route later, since all remaining routes are longer.
paragraphs: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source to all nodes when edge weights are non-negative. It repeatedly 'finalises' the closest unfinished node, then relaxes its outgoing edges to possibly improve its neighbours' tentative distances.

The greedy choice is valid precisely because weights are non-negative: once a node is the closest remaining, no future path (which must go through farther nodes) can beat its current distance. A min-priority-queue efficiently produces that closest node each step.
Negative edges break this guarantee — a later, longer-looking path could secretly be cheaper. For those, use Bellman-Ford.
intuition.keyIdea: Always finalise the nearest unsettled node; with non-negative weights its distance can't be improved later.

steps.title: Initialise
steps.detail: dist[src] = 0, all others ∞. Push (0, src) into a min-heap.

steps.title: Pop the closest
steps.detail: Extract the smallest-distance node. If it's stale (distance worse than recorded), skip it. Otherwise it's finalised.

steps.title: Relax edges
steps.detail: For each neighbour v: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v).

steps.title: Repeat
steps.detail: Continue until the heap is empty; dist now holds all shortest distances.

codes.source:
import heapq

def dijkstra(n, adj, src):           # adj[u] = [(v, w), ...]
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    pq = [(0, src)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                 # stale entry
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
    return dist

complexity.timeReason: Each edge can trigger a heap push; heap operations cost log V.

pitfalls: Fails with negative edge weights — use Bellman-Ford instead.
Skip stale heap entries (d > dist[u]) or you'll do redundant work.
Use a 64-bit distance type to avoid overflow on large weights.

dryRun.input: Source A; edges A-C(2), C-B(1), A-B(4), B-D(5), D-E(2), E-F(3)
dryRun.clickMoment: B was tentatively 4 via the direct edge, but popping C first relaxed it to 3 (A→C→B). Because C was closer, its relaxations were trustworthy — the greedy order guarantees correctness.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.statement: Time for a signal to reach all nodes from a source.
problems.hint: Dijkstra; answer is the max finalised distance.

approach: Non-negative weights, so Dijkstra is optimal. Use a min-heap keyed by distance from the source k.
Pop the closest unsettled node, relax its edges. The answer is the largest settled distance, or -1 if some node never settles.

problems.title: Path With Minimum Effort
problems.statement: Minimise the maximum height difference along a path.
problems.hint: Dijkstra where 'distance' is the path's max edge (min-max).

approach: Edge 'cost' is the absolute height difference, and a path's cost is its largest single step. This is a min-max (bottleneck) shortest path — Dijkstra works with max instead of sum.
Key cells by the minimum possible effort to reach them; relax with effort = max(currentEffort, |height diff|).

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.statement: Cheapest price with at most K stops.
problems.hint: Dijkstra with a stop-count state, or Bellman-Ford limited to K+1 relaxations.

approach: State is (node, stops used). A node may be revisited if we reach it with fewer stops, so we cannot prune purely by cost.
Dijkstra-style heap ordered by cost; carry the stop count and only expand while stops <= K. The first time we pop the destination it is optimal.

problems.title: Swim in Rising Water
problems.statement: Least time to swim from corner to corner as water rises.
problems.hint: Dijkstra/▢ over the grid minimising the maximum cell value on the path.

approach: You can move once the water level reaches the higher of two adjacent cells. The cost of a path is the maximum cell value on it — a bottleneck shortest path.
Dijkstra from (0,0) keying each cell by the minimum possible 'time' (max elevation) to reach it; answer is that value at the bottom-right corner.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
problems.statement: Count shortest paths from 0 to n−1.
problems.hint: Dijkstra while accumulating path counts on equal-distance relaxations.

approach: Run Dijkstra from 0, but additionally keep ways[v] = number of shortest paths to v.
When we find a strictly shorter distance, ways[v] = ways[u]; when we find an equally short one, ways[v] += ways[u]. Return ways[n-1] modulo 1e9+7.
